title: Designing Nearby Friends: Location Sharing with Pub/Sub
lesson:
A nearby friends feature shows which of your friends are within some distance and updates as they move. It differs from a proximity service for businesses: the points being searched are moving users, and only friends should be visible, so the query is not a geospatial search over a huge index but a fan-out of location updates to a small social graph.

A common design has each active user's client send periodic location updates over a persistent WebSocket connection. The server stores the latest location in a fast key-value store such as Redis with a TTL, so users who stop updating drop off naturally, and publishes the update to a per-user channel in a pub/sub system. Each user's WebSocket handler subscribes to the channels of their friends who have the feature enabled, so when a friend moves, the update is delivered, and the receiving side computes the distance and shows the friend only if it is within the radius.

Scale comes from sharding the pub/sub channels, for example with consistent hashing across a cluster of Redis pub/sub servers by user id, and from keeping the work proportional to active users rather than total users. Fan-out cost grows with friend count, so systems cap the number of friends tracked or send updates less often when users move slowly. Location history, if kept, goes to a separate write-optimized store, because the real-time path only needs the latest position.

Since pub/sub is fire-and-forget, a missed message is acceptable: the next location update arrives seconds later and supersedes it. This is why durability is not required for the live channel, and why a lightweight in-memory pub/sub is a good fit. Privacy controls such as opt-in sharing and the ability to hide are essential, and should be checked on the subscribe path.

questions.prompt: Why is a lost location update on the live pub/sub channel generally acceptable?
options: A newer update arrives within seconds and supersedes it
questions.explanation: Only the latest position matters for the live view, so occasional losses are quickly healed by the next update.

questions.prompt: Storing the latest location in Redis with a ____ lets inactive users disappear automatically.
questions.explanation: A TTL expires stale entries when a user stops sending updates.

questions.prompt: In this design, the cost of delivering one user's movement grows with the number of their friends who are subscribed.
questions.explanation: Each update fans out to every subscribed friend, which is why systems cap tracked friends or reduce update frequency.

questions.prompt: Order the flow of one location update.
items: Friends' WebSocket handlers receive the update and check distance
Client sends location over its WebSocket
Server saves the latest location with a TTL
Server publishes the update to the user's pub/sub channel
questions.explanation: The update is received, stored, published, and finally filtered by distance on the receiving side.

questions.prompt: How can the pub/sub layer be scaled to many users?
options: Use a single channel for all users
Shard channels across servers, for example by consistent hashing on user id
Store every update in a relational table first
questions.explanation: Sharding channels by user id spreads subscription and publish load across a cluster.
